strengths: Principled and well-structured taxonomy: The benchmark bridges composition (structured around scene graph primitives: instances, attributes, relations, and text rendering) and reasoning (rooted in the philosophical tripartite framework of deductive, inductive, and abductive inference), covering 12 well-defined dimensions.

Meaningful step toward real-world complexity: Unlike prior benchmarks that test isolated 1-to-1 associations or sparse scenes, T2I-COREBENCH increases compositional density (~20 elements per prompt) and reasoning depth (compound/sequential causal chains and multi-premise puzzles).

Extensive experimental evaluation: Benchmarking 27 contemporary T2I generative models across diffusion, autoregressive, and unified paradigms (including recent closed-source models such as Imagen 4 and GPT-Image) offers an informative snapshot of current T2I capabilities.

Granular checklist-based evaluation protocol: Decomposing evaluation into ~13,500 atomic yes/no verification questions helps make MLLM-based visual QA evaluation much more interpretable and objective compared to direct Likert-scale scoring.
weaknesses: Incomplete human alignment on reasoning dimensions: The human validation study in Section 4.3 is restricted solely to the four compositional dimensions (MI, MA, MR, TR). The authors justify this by arguing that reasoning decomposes into visual elements, but detecting subtle, indirect visual traces of multi-step inference (e.g., abductive clues or counterfactual states) often poses unique perceptual and context-dependent challenges for MLLM evaluators.

Discrepancies across MLLM evaluators: As shown by comparing Table 2 (Gemini 2.5 Flash) and Table 4 (Qwen2.5-VL-72B), absolute scores shift noticeably across evaluators (e.g., Gemini gives lower composition scores across several models compared to Qwen). A deeper investigation into evaluator bias and calibration across model families would strengthen the evaluation's authority.

Lack of qualitative error analysis: While Section 4 notes that qualitative case studies are underway, the main paper currently lacks visual examples of model failures. Showing concrete visual comparisons of where models succeed or fail across different reasoning types would greatly enrich the empirical insights.

Uniform weighting of atomic checklist questions: The benchmark averages binary outcomes across checklist items without weighting central versus peripheral elements. Failing to depict a primary causal agent is penalized the same as missing an incidental background object.

strengths: Principled and comprehensive taxonomy: The paper grounds its evaluation framework in established concepts—scene graph theory (instance, attribute, relation) for composition and the philosophical tripartite framework (deductive, inductive, abductive) for reasoning—defining 12 distinct dimensions that overcome the heuristic categorizations of earlier benchmarks.

Focus on high compositional density and multi-hop reasoning: Unlike existing benchmarks that evaluate simple one-to-one or isolated attributes, the benchmark tests scenes with high instance/attribute density (~20-25 elements) and complex causal/inferential chains (e.g., one-to-many and many-to-one reasoning).

Extensive and rigorous empirical evaluation: The authors benchmark 27 modern T2I models (diffusion, autoregressive, and unified architectures, alongside top closed-source models), providing valuable empirical insights such as the persistent bottleneck in reasoning versus composition and the trade-offs of explicit chain-of-thought prompt rewriting (e.g., BAGEL vs. BAGEL w/ Think).

Atomic checklist-based evaluation with human alignment validation: Decomposing evaluation into ~13,500 atomic yes/no visual questions significantly reduces the ambiguity and error propagation of holistic MLLM scoring. The authors support this setup with a human alignment study across 10 MLLMs, reporting balanced accuracy.
weaknesses: Potential acquiescence bias in checklist design: As noted in Section 3.2, checklist items are framed such that the intended answer for a faithful depiction is always 'Yes'. MLLM evaluators frequently suffer from positive confirmation bias (acquiescence bias). Incorporating explicitly negative control questions would make the automated evaluation significantly more robust against false positives.

Limitations of MLLM visual perception under high visual density: In scenes containing 20–30 dense instances or fine-grained spatial/attribute relations, vision-language models (even Gemini 2.5 Flash or Qwen2.5-VL-72B) are known to struggle with grounding and small-object detection. Table 3 shows balanced accuracies around 71–81%, indicating a ~20–30% error margin in the judge itself, which may distort rankings.

Relatively modest sample size per subcategory: Although the overall benchmark contains 1,080 prompts, this translates to only 90 prompts per dimension (with 30 prompts per source LRM). A larger test set per specific reasoning sub-type would increase statistical confidence.

Draft artifacts and missing links: The manuscript contains noticeable submission oversights, such as an empty project page link on Page 1 ('Our project page: .') and explicit placeholders in Section 4 ('Additional experimental results ... are actively being conducted in progress and will be included in the next version'), reflecting a somewhat unpolished final draft.

strengths: Principled and comprehensive taxonomy: Grounding the composition evaluation in scene graphs (instance, attribute, relation) and the reasoning evaluation in philosophical inference frameworks (deductive, inductive, abductive) provides a structured and theoretically motivated benchmark.

Emphasis on complexity: Addressing the limitations of prior benchmarks that focus on low-density scenes and single-step one-to-one reasoning by scaling up to dense prompts (~20 elements) and multi-step / compound reasoning scenarios.

Extensive experimental evaluation: Evaluating 27 diverse T2I models (diffusion, autoregressive, and unified architectures across both open- and closed-source models) offers a timely and holistic snapshot of current state-of-the-art capabilities.

Fine-grained evaluation protocol with validation: Decomposing prompts into ~13,500 atomic yes/no checklist verification questions reduces evaluation ambiguity and is supported by a human alignment study across 10 MLLM evaluators using balanced accuracy.
weaknesses: Evaluator accuracy gap: As shown in Table 3, the chosen evaluator (Gemini 2.5 Flash) achieves ~81.1% balanced accuracy against human annotations, and the open-source alternative (Qwen2.5-VL-72B) achieves ~71.1%. An error rate around 19–29% in the evaluation judge introduces non-trivial noise into model ranking and per-category scores, particularly on subtle visual elements and relational attributes.

Checklist polarity / acquiescence bias: The checklist questions are formulated such that the target correct answer is uniformly 'Yes'. While this simplifies verification, MLLMs are known to exhibit varying degrees of positive affirmation / yes-bias, which could artificially inflate scores on certain models or dimensions.

Reliance on synthetic LLM-generated prompts: Although human verification by expert annotators is conducted, generating prompts and checklists primarily via Claude 4, Gemini 2.5 Pro, and OpenAI o3 may introduce synthetic prompt phrasing biases or unrealistic synthetic constraints that do not reflect human user distribution.

Lack of qualitative diagnostic analysis: The paper is heavily dominated by tabular metrics. Including visual examples of model failures across key reasoning categories (such as logical premise contradiction vs. reconstructive failure) in the main paper would substantially improve interpretability and diagnostic value.

strengths: Principled and comprehensive taxonomy: The paper grounds its evaluation in scene graph theory for composition (instance, attribute, relation) and formal philosophical reasoning frameworks (deductive, inductive, abductive), yielding a well-structured 12-dimensional taxonomy that substantially broadens the evaluation scope beyond existing T2I benchmarks.

High benchmark complexity: Unlike prior benchmarks characterized by sparse objects and simple one-to-one inferences, T2I-CoReBench pushes model limits with dense semantic scenes (~20 elements/prompt) and multi-step / many-to-one / one-to-many inferential chains.

Rigorous evaluation methodology: Pairing each prompt with an atomic, human-verified checklist (~13,500 yes/no questions total) provides an objective, granular, and reproducible evaluation protocol, minimizing holistic hallucination and error accumulation in automated MLLM scoring.

Extensive experimental evaluation: Evaluating 38 state-of-the-art models (diffusion, autoregressive, and unified architectures, covering both open- and closed-source systems) provides significant empirical value and community insights.

Insightful analysis on prompt rewriting: The experiment dissecting prompt rewriting (via OpenAI o3) reveals that while explicit text rewriting helps formal logical reasoning, it fails on multimodal visual counterfactuals (e.g., square wheels), highlighting the necessity of native visual reasoning in next-generation T2I systems.
weaknesses: Sample diversity per dimension: While the overall dataset contains 1,080 prompts and over 13,500 checklist items, dividing across 12 dimensions results in 90 prompts per dimension. Although the semantic density per prompt is high, expanding the breadth of prompts per specific reasoning type in future iterations would further strengthen robustness.

MLLM evaluation error margin: Although the authors provide a human alignment validation (achieving ~81% balanced accuracy with Gemini 2.5 Flash), evaluating high-density scenes with up to 35 entities remains challenging for current vision-language models, which could introduce minor false negatives on crowded visual details.

Uniform weighting of checklist items: The current scoring calculates the mean accuracy across checklist questions, which implicitly treats peripheral background details with equal importance as central semantic reasoning outcomes.

strengths: Principled and comprehensive taxonomy: Grounding the composition evaluation in scene-graph theory (instance, attribute, relation) and reasoning in formal inference philosophy (deductive, inductive, and abductive) brings much-needed structure and rigour compared to ad-hoc benchmarks.

Scale and depth of evaluation: The empirical study evaluates 38 modern T2I models spanning diffusion, autoregressive, and unified architectures across open-source and proprietary systems, providing a valuable snapshot of current model capabilities.

Careful checklist design and validation: Decomposing complex prompt requirements into ~13,500 atomic yes/no verification questions makes MLLM-based scoring objective and reproducible. The inclusion of a human alignment study (reporting balanced accuracy across 15+ MLLMs) lends strong credibility to the chosen evaluator.

Insightful analysis of prompt rewriting: Section 4.3 thoughtfully investigates whether reasoning failures stem solely from text comprehension bottlenecks or inherent visual biases, showing that text-only prompt rewriting fails on strong visual priors (e.g., drawing square wheels).

High quality of presentation and transparency: The manuscript is exceptionally well organized, clearly written, and accompanied by comprehensive appendices detailing prompts, guidelines, and qualitative examples.
weaknesses: Potential evaluator bias and dependence on closed APIs: Using Gemini 2.5 Flash as the primary evaluator across all benchmarks poses risks of subtle model bias toward specific outputs (especially models from the same family or those trained on similar synthetic distributions), even though open-source alternatives are reported on the leaderboard.

Dataset scale per sub-dimension: While the total question count is large (~13,500 checklist items), the benchmark contains 90 prompts per dimension (30 per LRM source). A slightly larger prompt sample per dimension would strengthen statistical confidence.

Distinction between textual reasoning and visual generation: Several reasoning dimensions (e.g., Logical Reasoning puzzles and Generalization in-context rules) heavily test the reasoning capability of the text encoder rather than the vision generation pipeline itself, though the prompt rewriting experiment partially addresses this.

strengths: Comprehensive and well-structured taxonomy: The benchmark bridges visual composition (grounded in scene graph concepts: instances, attributes, relations, text) and multimodal reasoning (grounded in philosophical inference categories: deductive, inductive, abductive) across 12 fine-grained dimensions.
Extensive and up-to-date empirical evaluation: Benchmarks 38 distinct T2I models spanning diffusion, autoregressive, and unified architectures, as well as state-of-the-art commercial APIs.
Fine-grained checklist methodology: The use of ~13,500 atomic yes/no questions enables granular and objective verification of both explicit compositional elements and implicit reasoning outcomes.

Insightful analysis of prompt rewriting vs. native reasoning: Section 4.3 and Table 4 provide meaningful analysis showing where textual chain-of-thought rewriting helps (e.g., pure logical deduction) and where visual/multimodal biases prevent success (e.g., rendering counterfactuals like square wheels).
weaknesses: Reliance on MLLM-based automated evaluation: Although the authors provide a human alignment study (balanced accuracy around 81% for Gemini 2.5 Flash), MLLM evaluators are known to struggle with fine spatial reasoning, precise counting, and subtle visual anomalies, which could introduce systematic noise into the scores.

Synthetic prompt distribution: Prompts and checklists are generated using frontier reasoning models (o3, Claude Sonnet 4, Gemini 2.5 Pro). Although human-verified by graduate students, synthetic prompts often differ in style and pragmatic intent from real-world human user prompts.

Modest sample size per category: With 1,080 prompts divided across 12 dimensions and 3 generating LRMs, each specific subcategory comprises 90 prompts (30 per LRM), which is relatively small for drawing definitive fine-grained statistical conclusions.

Binary checklist bias: Designing all checklist questions so that the ground-truth target is always 'Yes' can interact unfavorably with the prior biases or affirmative tendencies of MLLM evaluators, despite the negative filtering instruction ('ambiguity equals no').
